rv.q: The director, Mark Lamos, hasn’t elicited performances that might give the relationship between Cornelia and Walker the intriguing emotional undertow suggested in the script...Were we to see something more dark and urgent in his mission, the play would cut a little deeper. Mr. Gurney springs a few surprises, some more plausible than others."
The play fills out the season, but no more.
Mark Lamos’ production goes down easy, but it’s also nutrient-free and meandering.
It is a buoyant comedy that also contains some startlingly shrewd observations about wealth, the nature of trust, and the prospect of aging with dignity.
At this point, while certainly flawed, the lightly philosophical comedy can provide a pleasing, if not totally satisfying time.
Both make the play fun to take in from moment to moment, even though those moments don’t ultimately add up to one of the playwright’s best works.
In the end, the comedy (?)--a co-production of the SignatureTheatre and the Westport Country Playhouse, where Mark Lamos, who directed, is artistic director--is a minor trifle.
But neither the song nor the set-up has much life left in it, even ironically.
At just 75 minutes, the show strains patience, credulity and goodwill.
Why this play is being produced, when there are boatloads of good plays out there pining away for a friendly nod, is a mystery.
If you want an enjoyable, light visit to the theatre, then you can do a lot worse than ‘Love and Money’.
Cornelia isn’t as naive and blinded by liberal guilt as as she appears.
About the best thing to say about the places to which Gurney takes Cornelia and Walker is that they contain more than a couple of odd surprises.
“Love & Money” is definitely a production with more style than substance.
It has its moments, but it needs work.
If you like A.R. Gurney, you will love this WASPY throwback comedy.

While it is sadly just too derivative and unimaginative to provide a satisfactory theatrical experience, it remains a delight to see how Anderman has grown as an actress and willingly throws herself in each part with an honesty and believability that is not apparent on the page.
Unfortunately, the play fails to deliver on that early promise.
Sadly, “Love & Money,” really needed some more time out of town (besides a brief summer run at the Westport Country Playhouse) before hitting the Big Apple.
LOVE & MONEY, a slight, formulaic comedy, briskly staged by Mark Lamos, has arrived at the Signature...
Three weeks of "previews" at Westport did not improve a play that has not progressed much beyond a draft.
